name: Diffusion of Innovations
statement: New ideas and technologies spread through a social system over time via distinct adopter categories, from innovators to laggards.
meaning: Diffusion of innovations explains how, why, and at what rate new ideas, practices, and products spread among members of a social system. It models adoption as a process moving through knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation, and confirmation, rather than a single event.
mechanism: Rogers synthesised findings from over 500 earlier diffusion studies across anthropology, sociology, education, and medicine. Adopters are sorted into five categories by willingness to try an innovation — innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, and laggards — producing an S-shaped adoption curve over time as opinion leaders and social networks pass the innovation along.

examples.text: Ryan and Gross’s 1943 study of Iowa farmers adopting hybrid seed corn over more than a decade became a foundational case that helped establish diffusion research and shaped Rogers’s later synthesis.

Rogers documented a failed public-health campaign in Los Molinos, Peru, to persuade residents to boil drinking water, which stalled due to cultural beliefs and social resistance despite the health benefits.

In the 1980s–90s, organisations adopting computer technology were shown to be held back less by lack of awareness than by lack of technical knowledge, illustrating the implementation stage of the model.

whyItMatters: The theory gives public-health campaigns, marketers, and technology firms a structured way to target early adopters and opinion leaders to accelerate uptake. It remains one of the most widely cited frameworks in communication and development studies.
limits: The model was built mainly from studies of individual, voluntary adoption and can understate structural, economic, or coercive factors. Critics note the adopter categories are statistical constructs based on a normal distribution rather than fixed personality types, and real adoption often does not fit a clean S-curve.
misreadings: "Early adopter" and "laggard" are often used as fixed personal identities or insults, when Rogers intended them as descriptive statistical categories relative to a specific innovation and social system, not permanent traits.
origin: Proposed by rural-sociology professor Everett M. Rogers in his 1962 book "Diffusion of Innovations," synthesising over 500 prior diffusion studies.
